quote: Are you trying to buy her house?
stewart_read: The customer assumes this is a predatory call targeting his elderly mother's home, a scam-adjacent anxiety distinct from the standard 'how did you get my number' trust probe — it's specifically about protecting a vulnerable parent from house-buying schemes. The rep answers 'No.' flatly without acknowledging why that assumption exists.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged a quick denial was sufficient since the customer moved on immediately at 00:16 without further pushback.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to briefly name the concern ('I get why you'd think that, we're not connected to any of those calls') before pivoting — a half-second acknowledgment costs nothing and builds trust faster than a bare denial.

quote: No. No. We usually, whenever I get calls regarding Rita, which is she's my mom, It's somebody trying to buy her house.
stewart_read: This is the customer explicitly disclosing a recurring harassment pattern targeting his mother — a trust gift similar to the scam-encounter disclosures flagged elsewhere in the corpus (protocols.scam_encounter_reference). The rep's next line pivots straight into the pitch ('Okay. Well, we actually...') without acknowledging the disclosure at all.

coaching_implication: Flag this as a missed one-line acknowledgment ('sorry you keep getting those calls, that's rough') — costs three seconds, meaningfully differentiates Ion from the predatory callers the customer is describing.

quote: Is it like, I live in the middle of the city. Would that require, like, permits permits for city stuff?
stewart_read: Customer asks a legitimate permit/logistics question. Rep answers directly with a guess ('Not that I'm aware of') instead of using the universal escape hatch to defer to the specialist, which is the schema-correct move for closer-tier technical content.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's guess was low-stakes and didn't derail the call, so this could be read as harmless small talk rather than true scope creep — but the schema treats any answered technical/logistics question as a miss regardless of outcome.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to use 'that's exactly what our specialist will walk you through' on permit/logistics questions rather than answering from uncertainty — an incorrect guess here could resurface as a broken promise at the closer stage.

quote: It's my mom right now. It's a it's a transferred upon desk setup.
stewart_read: The customer reveals his mother is the actual titleholder (transfer-on-death setup), making her the legal decision-maker, not him. The rep never asks whether the mother needs to be on the appointment or the eventual closer call — treating the son as the sole point of contact throughout the rest of the call.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be planning to loop the mother in later once the bill photo comes back, since she's asleep and unreachable right now — a deferred-not-skipped inclusion.
coaching_implication: This needs to be explicit, not assumed. Coach the rep to say something like 'since she's the owner, let's make sure she's part of the appointment too' — right now the appointment risk is that a non-owner books time without owner buy-in, which the closer will discover cold.

quote: Let me think. But oh, do you or your mom have a credit score over 670?
stewart_read: Rep runs the credit qualifier correctly and gets a clean answer, but asks it of 'you or your mom' without clarifying whose credit will actually be pulled given the mother is the titleholder — a loose end tied to the same ownership ambiguity from 02:49.
alternative_hypothesis: This may be immaterial if Ion's underwriting allows either party's credit to qualify a transfer-on-death property, but that's not established on the call.
coaching_implication: Minor, but worth a note to the closer — confirm which party's credit is actually being run before the proposal stage.

stewart_read: The customer surfaces a real access barrier — he can't get the bill without waking/reaching his mother. Rep handles this reasonably by pivoting to a text-later plan, but the call ends without ever converting that into a locked appointment day/time.

quote: Okay. If I text you, could you, talk to her and then get that usage, and then we can get you on the schedule?
stewart_read: The call closes on a soft, unlocked plan — a text will be sent, a photo might come back 'later this afternoon,' and scheduling happens after that, with no committed callback time from the rep and no button-up elements (hour block, no-driving, handshake) delivered at all.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the bill is genuinely required before scheduling (paid-lead bill rule), deferring the appointment itself may be correct procedure — but even so, the rep could have locked a specific callback time rather than leaving it purely to the customer's initiative.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to always end with a rep-owned next step: 'I'll call you back at [time] today to get that photo and get you scheduled' — right now the plan depends entirely on the customer remembering to text back.
